---
title: "Oh, SNAP! Exploring Retailer Availability, SNAP Participation, and Migration in the US"
date: 2026-04-29
author: Brooke Proctor, Emery Kerani, Tiffany Truong
---

Motivation & Finalized research question: 
Access to SNAP benefits can have huge benefits: chiefly, each dollar allocated to SNAP can generate $1.79 in economic activity (FRAC, 2026). Furthermore, food insecurity among children fell by roughly 33 percent after their families received benefits for about six months (Mabli and Worthington, 2014). At the same time, millions of immigrant households have limited or uncertain access to adequate food (Health University of Utah, 2017). This highlights an important relationship between migration and SNAP usage/SNAP access, which we wanted to focus on because Salem is the official refugee resettlement city in Oregon. 
This knowledge led us to our final research questions: “What retailers accept EBT/SNAP benefits, and does the number of retailers accepting these benefits change based on county poverty levels?”  We were also interested in exploring the secondary question, “is the number of retailers that accept EBT/SNAP benefits correlated with the net migration level of counties?” Our final SQL queries and dashboard utilize almost all of our variables from each dataset to visualize and understand the relationships between EBT/SNAP retailers, county poverty levels and migration.
Finalized pipeline architecture 
Our Data Sources:
To understand our research question, we needed to first find data related to SNAP retailers, SNAP usage/participation across different counties and migration across counties.  The data on SNAP usage in counties comes from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.  The U.S. The Department of Agriculture also includes data on authorized SNAP retailers across the United States. Additionally, our migration data comes from the U.S. American Community Survey (ACS) and includes net migration for each ACS period and state/county. 
Ingestion: 
Our data is not being ingested continuously; it is composed of several CSVs obtained through one-time downloads, which is highly repeatable. We have cleaned our data to contain only the columns we deemed important to our ERD, which is also reproducible.  One conflict with this is that if the data is no longer publicly available on the government websites we downloaded it from, it may not be repeatable.
Orchestration
For the scope of our project, this is just a download from a CSV that is put into beekeeper using the “table from CSV” functionality. There was a significant amount of data cleaning in the parts in between, but it was all done using scripts, so it is easily repeatable. A few queries were run to join and summarize the data, including the creation of Views to achieve some of our desired queries.

Serving
We used the queries mentioned above to create a Grafana dashboard. This dashboard tells a story about migration, poverty, and food access at the state and county levels, over time. This includes many bar graphs and scatter plots that show trends between variables, such as rural populations and the amount of stores with SNAP accessibility. 
Finalized schema and transformations: 
Our final schema includes four tables. The first table is titled “migrations” and includes rows on the migration for each county; the primary key is the American Community Survey  (ACS)  period. Our second table is titled “retailers” and  it includes information on the retailers including, name, store type, county and authorization dates. Its primary key is a surrogate id representing each retailer and SNAP authorization period. Its foreign key is the acs_period_id. Our third table is the “snaps” table that includes demographic data relating to total population and participation in SNAP.  The primary key is a surrogate key titled “n” to represent county and acs_period and the foreign key is the acs_period_id. Finally, we included a look up table for the ACS periods. Finalized limitations and future work: 
One of our big constraints is time data. We have a very limited window of dates that all line up. There are some other sources that have a longer time frame, but the data is stored in a less intuitive way and would rely on more data cleaning, which did not seem feasible for this project. There is a lot more that can be done with more data, and there would likely be trends in the data following elections or important legislature changes, that at this point we simply cannot access. 

Finalized results summary: 
To display the results of our queries, we created a dashboard in Grafana. Several interesting findings emerged from our graphs, one of the most significant of which was that rural counties actually tended to have more SNAP retailers (which we offer an explanation for below). Unsurprisingly, in our fourth graph we found that the absolute number of people on SNAP is related to the number of SNAP retailers, but this relationship becomes murkier when using standardized versions of the variables (retailers per 1,000 people and share of the population on SNAP). In the standardized version of this graph, it’s easier to pick out that the counties with the highest proportion of poverty tend to be rural, and the relationship between SNAP participation and retailers becomes less clear. In our next set of graphs, we see that rural counties tend to see bigger changes in their population (by percentage), but the relationship between migration and number of retailers is slightly obscured by clustering at the lower end of the number of retailers scale. Completing the trifecta of variables we’re interested in, our graphs of migration and SNAP participation show very dynamics as those we’ve already discussed. Our final graph examines each of these three variables by state to compare urban and rural counties, and will be discussed more below.
After completing our dashboard and running our queries,  we found correlational relationships between variables in our datasets and answered our original research questions. The first notable relationship is between SNAP retailers and poverty in counties. As SNAP retailers increase, poverty also increases. In fact, our findings show a 0.929 correlation between SNAP retailers and poverty in counties. This indicates a strong positive correlation between SNAP retailers and the level of poverty. This is likely a result of population changes. As populations increase within counties, SNAP retailers or the number of grocery stores/retailers are also likely to increase. Additionally, increases in poverty are also often associated with population growth over time in a county.
In terms of the correlation between SNAP retailers and migration, as SNAP retailers increase the migration into the county also decreases. Our findings report a -0.509 correlation between retailers and migration into the county. This indicates a moderately strong negative correlation between SNAP retailers and migration. In a similar vein, we also found a -0.449 correlation between SNAP participation and migration, which makes sense given how highly correlated SNAP participation and the number of SNAP retailers are.
While our initial questions were not necessarily focused on geography, this project also revealed that rurality/urbanity play a large role in the availability of resources as well as migration. Across all states, rural counties (those with 50,000 people or less) were generally more likely to see outward migration on average, while urban counties were more likely to see population gains. In addition, rural counties generally had higher shares of their populations on SNAP, and perhaps counter-intuitively also had greater access to SNAP retailers per 1,000 people (which we chalk up to these retailers simply serving a smaller number of people). 
Reflection: 

	We learned so much. Firstly, normalizing data for an in-class exercise is difficult, but not nearly as hard as it is when working with several real-world, messy datasets. We struggled immensely to create an ERD that looked good—not even necessarily normalized, just reliable and readable. We completely threw normalization out the window because our time data is such a headache to work with. Some of the data is aggregated to a five year period, which makes joining the data very difficult! This lack of normalization means that it is a bigger file that is storing NA’s, which made Railway sort of difficult to work with at first too, because of the memory limit. We chose to prioritize simplicity, which came with a very real tradeoff. If we were to do it again, we would work to create a normalized table, which would make much of our work significantly easier. 
Filtering the data was another instance of a tradeoff. We removed a large chunk of the retailer data so that we were not running into memory issues in Railway. This meant that we had an even more limited scope of years to look into. We have no time series data to show off precisely because we got rid of so much of it in cleaning and joining the data. 
Our junction table also created quite the headache. This table was accidentally creating thousands more rows than we expected, because the junction was not normalized. I think to get there we would have had to make another separate table for the junction table, which we just didn’t have the time to play with. It did make a really strong case for normalization, though.
In navigating the challenges and surprises from this project, we learned several things. Firstly, making ERDs is hard.  Real data is often messier and has extra issues when time information is incorporated. To navigate this we ended up making several versions of our ERD.
We also learned that there are some difficulties using the Beekeeper import tables. It is a little trickier than anticipated because it is really serious about not having duplicates in a way we didn’t see before with COPY statements. It took us a very long time to get the SNAP data, in particular, into a staging table. 
There were several very minor issues we ran into that presented major roadblocks in the process of getting our database up and running. For example, you should always be careful about spaces… we spent the better part of the afternoon wondering why two columns weren’t joining on each other, only to discover that there was a space before every state abbreviation because of the way one column had been transformed.
As for teamwork, we are an awesome team. Tiffany is so good at doing things quickly and efficiently. She also is very very good at finding data that rocks. Emery is the best Grafana user in the world so that is very helpful. Brooke is literally the coolest person ever and was a great leader for the team. We worked very well as a team and think there was appropriate division of labor.
